results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No, creatures phasing back in do not trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities. Phasing is a static ability that modifies the rules of the untap step. When a permanent phases in, its status changes to "phased in," and the game treats it as though it exists again on the battlefield. However, the phasing event itself does not cause a permanent to change zones or control, and zone-change triggers do not occur when a permanent phases in or out. This is because the game checks for trigger conditions based on objects that exist immediately after an event, and phasing in is not considered an event that causes a permanent to enter the battlefield.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When a creature with trample deals combat damage, its controller first assigns lethal damage to any creatures blocking it. After all blocking creatures have been assigned lethal damage, any excess damage can be assigned to the player, planeswalker, or battle the creature is attacking. If a creature has deathtouch, any amount of damage it deals to a creature is considered lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage. This means that if a creature with both trample and deathtouch is blocked, its controller only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to satisfy the lethal damage requirement, and the rest of the damage can be assigned to the defending player or planeswalker. This interaction is governed by the rules for trample [702.19b] and deathtouch [702.2c]. Deathtouch functions regardless of the zone the source is in [702.2d]. If a creature with deathtouch deals damage, and that creature is destroyed as a state-based action, it is still considered to have dealt damage with deathtouch [704.5h].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes, Storm is a triggered ability that can be countered. Storm is defined as a triggered ability that functions on the stack, meaning it can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities [702.40a, 113.9].

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: Yes, you can use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a Commander deck even if only one of the colors in the hybrid symbol is present in the commander's color identity. A hybrid mana symbol is considered to be all of its component colors [107.4e]. Therefore, a card with a hybrid mana symbol like {R/G} has both red and green in its color identity. According to rule [903.5c], each card in a Commander deck must have a color identity that is found within the color identity of the deck's commander. If your commander's color identity is red, a card with {R/G} in its mana cost would be legal because red is part of the {R/G} color identity, and red is present in your commander's color identity. Similarly, if your commander's color identity is green, the {R/G} card would also be legal. If your commander's color identity is red and green, the {R/G} card is legal. If your commander's color identity is only red, and you want to include a card with {R/G} in its mana cost, that card's color identity is red and green. Since green is not in your commander's color identity, that card would not be legal. However, if the card's color identity is only red, and it has a hybrid mana symbol that can be paid with red mana, it would be legal. The rule states that a card can be included if *every* color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck's commander [903.5c].

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, which means no spells can be cast, no abilities can be activated, and no actions can be taken. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held until the next time a player would receive priority, which is typically during the upkeep step. The untap step is the first step of the beginning phase and ends when all its specified actions are completed.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. A creature remains an attacking creature until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first [Attacking Creature]. The end of combat step is part of the combat phase [End of Combat Step].

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Playing a land is a special action that does not use the stack and is not a spell [305.1, 701.18a]. An object that is both a land and another card type, such as an artifact land, can only be played as a land and cannot be cast as a spell [300.2a, 305.9, Artifact Land]. The term "play a card" means to play that card as a land or cast it as a spell, whichever is appropriate [701.18b, Play].

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: No, you cannot sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves. The evoke ability states that when the permanent enters the battlefield, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it [702.74a]. This sacrifice is part of the resolution of the evoke triggered ability itself. You cannot sacrifice the creature before this ability resolves because the game state does not allow for actions to be taken between the steps of a spell or ability's resolution [500.12]. Therefore, the sacrifice required by the evoke ability happens as that ability resolves.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, if a card loses all abilities, that includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are a type of ability, and effects that remove abilities remove all instances of them [113.10b]. Keyword abilities are defined as abilities that are common or would require too much space to define on the card, and are listed by name [702.1, 702.1d].

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you are at your maximum hand size. However, if you are at your maximum hand size at the beginning of your cleanup step, you will discard cards until you are at your maximum hand size. If your library is empty and you are instructed to draw a card, you will draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. If an effect offers you the choice to draw a card and you have no cards in your library, you can choose to do so, unless another effect prevents you from drawing cards. If an effect moves cards from your library to your hand without using the word "draw," you have not drawn those cards, even if your library is empty.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters, it is put into its owner's graveyard. This is a state-based action, meaning it happens automatically whenever the game state meets certain conditions and does not use the stack. The number of loyalty counters on a planeswalker on the battlefield indicates how much loyalty it has, and a planeswalker with 0 loyalty is put into its owner's graveyard. Damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from it.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No, noncreature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" specifically applies to creatures and planeswalkers being put into a graveyard from the battlefield [Dies]. Noncreature permanents, including artifacts, are not subject to the state-based actions that cause creatures to die, such as having lethal damage marked on them [704.5g], [704.5h], or having toughness 0 or less [704.5f]. If a noncreature artifact is put into its owner's graveyard for any reason other than being destroyed, it has not been "destroyed" [701.8b].

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: If you should draw a card when your library is empty, you will lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. This is because attempting to draw a card from an empty library is a state-based action that causes a player to lose the game. If an effect replaces the card draw, that replacement effect will still apply even if there are no cards to draw. If an effect moves cards from your library to your hand without using the word "draw," you have not drawn those cards, and this distinction matters if your library is empty.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The steps of the combat phase, in order, are: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped if no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking [506.1]. There are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1].

As the defending player, you generally do not have priority during the beginning of combat step unless a spell or ability instructs you to take an action [117.1]. In a two-player game, the nonactive player is the defending player [506.2]. In a multiplayer game, the active player chooses one opponent to be the defending player during the beginning of combat step, unless all opponents automatically become defending players [703.4h, 507.1, 506.2a].

You will have priority during the declare blockers step to declare blockers [703.4j, 509.1]. After the combat damage step, the active player gets priority during the end of combat step [511.1].

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities do not use the stack, which means they cannot be responded to. Activated mana abilities resolve immediately after they are activated [605.3b], and triggered mana abilities resolve immediately after the ability that triggered them, without waiting for priority [605.4a]. This is because mana abilities are special in that they don't use the stack [113.4].

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: You cannot respond to a cost being paid. Paying a cost is a step in casting a spell or activating an ability that does not use the stack [508.1j, 509.1f]. Once a player has enough mana, they pay all costs in any order, and partial payments are not allowed [508.1j, 509.1f]. If a cost includes mana, the player paying the cost has a chance to activate mana abilities [118.2]. However, the act of paying the cost itself is not an action that can be responded to.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text: The layer system is a method used in Magic: The Gathering to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to objects. Continuous effects are those that are active continuously, not just for a moment. The game applies these effects in a series of layers and sublayers, ensuring that characteristics of objects are consistently determined. The process begins with the object's base characteristics, whether printed on a card or defined by an effect that created it [613.1]. Then, continuous effects are applied in a specific order of layers [613.1]. These layers include, but are not limited to, Layer 1 (rules and effects that modify copiable values, including copy effects and effects from merging with permanents) [613.1a, 613.2a], Layer 3 (text-changing effects) [613.1c], Layer 4 (type-changing effects) [613.1d], Layer 5 (color-changing effects) [613.1e], and Layer 7 (power and toughness changing effects, which has its own sublayers) [613.4]. Within each layer or sublayer, effects are typically applied in timestamp order, meaning earlier effects are applied before later ones [613.7]. However, dependency can alter this order [613.8]. If an effect applies to multiple layers, its parts are applied in their respective layers, and the effect continues to apply to the same objects even if the source of the effect is removed [613.6].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that applies when a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name. When this occurs, that player must choose one of the permanents to keep, and all the others are put into their owner's graveyard. This rule applies to any permanent with the supertype "legendary." Previously, planeswalkers were subject to a "planeswalker uniqueness rule," but this has been removed, and planeswalkers printed before this change now have the legendary supertype and are subject to the legend rule. In the Commander variant, each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as that deck's commander, and the legend rule still applies to these commanders.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text: Your creature dies as a state-based action after it has been marked with a lethal amount of damage. State-based actions are checked automatically whenever a player would receive priority, and they happen before a player receives priority. If a creature has damage marked on it equal to or greater than its toughness, it is destroyed as a state-based action, unless it regenerates. Damage marked on a creature remains until the cleanup step, at which point it is removed. However, the creature is destroyed as soon as state-based actions are checked after lethal damage has been dealt, not necessarily at the cleanup step.

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: Yes, you can cast your commander from exile in a Commander game, provided certain conditions are met. Rule [903.9] states that a commander may return to the command zone during a Commander game. Specifically, if a commander is in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone as a state-based action [704.6d, 903.9a]. Additionally, if a commander would be put into your hand or library from anywhere, you may put it into the command zone instead, which is a replacement effect [903.9b]. Once a commander is in the command zone, you may cast it from there, incurring an additional cost for each previous time it has been cast from the command zone that game [903.8]. Some cards also have abilities that allow them to be cast from exile, such as plotted cards [702.170d].

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text: During the cleanup step, all damage marked on permanents is removed, and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. This happens simultaneously. If the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size, they discard cards to reduce their hand size to that number. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated. However, if state-based actions would be performed or triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, those actions are performed, those abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player receives priority. If this happens, players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins.

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked throughout the game whenever a player would get priority [704.2], [117.5]. They are also checked at the beginning of each step and phase before turn-based actions are dealt with [703.3]. Additionally, state-based actions are checked during the cleanup step [704.3], [514.3a]. When state-based actions are checked, the game performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event [704.3]. If any state-based actions are performed, the check is repeated until no more state-based actions are performed [704.3]. State-based actions do not use the stack and happen automatically when certain conditions are met [704.1a], [704.1].

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: A player can concede the game at any time. Conceding a game immediately causes that player to leave that game and lose that game. This is an exception to the rule that card text overrides general rules; a player can always concede, even if a card's text would prevent it. In a Two-Headed Giant game, if a player concedes, their team leaves the game immediately and that team loses the game.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is the player whose turn it is [Active Player]. In a multiplayer game where opponents don't automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one of their opponents to be the defending player during the beginning of combat step [507.1]. If multiple players would make choices or take actions at the same time, the active player makes their choices first, followed by the nonactive players in turn order [101.4]. If the shared team turns option is used, the active team is the team whose turn it is [Active Team], and players on the active team make their choices before players on nonactive teams [805.6]. An ability that refers to the "active player" refers to a single active player, chosen by the ability's controller if there are multiple active players [805.9].

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When a player who is not the active player casts a spell, that player receives priority. This is because rule [117.3c] states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. The active player is the player whose turn it is [101.4].

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When the active player casts a spell, that player receives priority afterward. This is because rule [117.3c] states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Rule [117.1] clarifies that the player with priority may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes, you can hold priority to cast more spells after you've cast one or more spells. When you cast a spell, you receive priority afterward, allowing you to cast additional spells or activate abilities before passing priority to another player. This is because casting a spell is an action that grants you priority upon completion, as long as no other rule or effect prevents it. If you cast a spell or activate an ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack, the new spell or ability is cast "in response" to the earlier one and will resolve first. This process can continue as long as you have priority and are able to cast spells or activate abilities.

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text: Lore counters are put on Saga enchantments during the active player's precombat main phase. This is a turn-based action that does not use the stack. Additionally, some Sagas enter the battlefield with lore counters already on them due to replacement effects, either intrinsically or through the "Read Ahead" ability.

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect that does something later in the game, rather than immediately when the effect resolves. These abilities are created during the resolution of spells or abilities, or as a result of a replacement effect being applied. They typically contain the words "when," "whenever," or "at," though these words may not begin the ability itself. A delayed triggered ability will only trigger the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it has a stated duration. If the object the ability refers to is no longer in the zone it's expected to be in when the delayed triggered ability resolves, the ability won't affect it.

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells can have abilities. Specifically, instant and sorcery spells have spell abilities that are followed as instructions while they are resolving [113.3a]. These spell abilities usually function only while the instant or sorcery spell is on the stack [113.6]. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack are considered objects and can be countered by effects that counter abilities [113.1c, 113.9].

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can use a mana ability when a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second is a static ability that functions while the spell is on the stack, and it states that players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities [702.61a]. Mana abilities are subject to special rules and do not use the stack [113.4]. Specifically, you may activate an activated mana ability whenever you have priority, or whenever you are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment, even if it's in the middle of casting or resolving a spell or activating or resolving an ability [605.3a]. Triggered mana abilities also do not go on the stack and resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered them [605.4a].

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: When all players pass priority, Counterspell will resolve first because it is on top of the stack. Counterspell will then counter Divination, meaning Divination will be removed from the stack and will not resolve. This is because a countered spell does not resolve and none of its effects occur [701.6a]. Divination will be put into its owner's graveyard [701.6a].

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign at least 2 damage to the Vampire Nighthawk before you can assign any excess damage to the player. This is because the Vampire Nighthawk has a toughness of 3 [302.4b], and while deathtouch means any damage is lethal, trample requires you to assign lethal damage to the blocker first. Since the Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, any amount of damage you assign to it is considered lethal damage for the purpose of assigning damage [702.2c]. However, the rules for trample state that you must assign lethal damage to the blocking creature(s) before assigning excess damage to the player [702.19b]. In this scenario, the Vampire Nighthawk has a toughness of 3. Therefore, you must assign at least 3 damage to the Vampire Nighthawk to satisfy the lethal damage requirement for the blocker, even though deathtouch would normally destroy it with less damage. Once you have assigned 3 damage to the Vampire Nighthawk, any remaining damage from the Charging Rhino can be assigned to the player.

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text: The Monastery Swiftspear's prowess ability triggers when you cast Shardless Agent, which is a noncreature spell. This trigger goes on the stack on top of Shardless Agent. Then, Shardless Agent's cascade ability triggers and resolves, exiling cards until a nonland card with a lesser mana value is found. If a noncreature spell is cast as part of the cascade, that spell goes on the stack above the Shardless Agent. Since the prowess trigger is on top of the Shardless Agent, and the cascaded spell is also on top of the Shardless Agent, the prowess trigger will resolve before the cascaded spell. This is because the prowess trigger is on top of the stack, and the spell that caused it to trigger (Shardless Agent) is below it, and the cascaded spell is also below the prowess trigger. Therefore, the Monastery Swiftspear's prowess ability resolves before the cascaded spell.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: No, state-based actions do not make your opponent's Grizzly Bears die before your Lightning Bolt resolves. Lightning Bolt is an instant spell, and instants can be cast when a player has priority. State-based actions are checked only when a player would receive priority, or when an effect that ends the turn or combat phase occurs. Since Lightning Bolt is being cast, it will go on the stack, and then resolve before state-based actions are checked. After Lightning Bolt resolves and deals 3 damage to Grizzly Bears, the damage is marked on it. Then, state-based actions will be checked. Grizzly Bears has 2 damage marked on it, and its toughness is 2. Since the damage marked on it is not greater than or equal to its toughness, it will not be destroyed by state-based actions. If the damage had been lethal, it would have been destroyed as a state-based action after Lightning Bolt resolved, but before you would have received priority again.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text: When your upkeep step begins, both your Phyrexian Arena's triggered ability and your opponent's triggered ability trigger simultaneously because they both trigger "at the beginning of" the upkeep step [500.6]. These abilities are put onto the stack before either player receives priority [117.3a]. Since you are the active player, you will put your triggered ability on the stack first, and then your opponent will put their triggered ability on the stack [101.4]. This means your opponent's ability will resolve before yours [603.3b].

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: When you cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, that spell will go into your hand instead of your graveyard as it resolves [702.27a]. When Fork copies that spell, the copy is not considered to have been cast [Fork ruling #9]. Therefore, the copy of the spell does not have a card to return to your hand, and you will only get the original sorcery back into your hand because you paid its buyback cost. You will have one copy of the card back in your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. When a manifested card is turned face-down, it becomes a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, abilities, or mana cost. This is because it is a "face-down permanent" and not a "card" for the purposes of copying. When this creature dies, it is exiled by Mimic Vat. However, Mimic Vat's second ability states that it creates a token that is a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat. Since the manifested card was a creature and not a card with the characteristics of Lightning Bolt, the token created will not be a copy of Lightning Bolt. Furthermore, rule [111.12] states that if an effect instructs a player to create a token that is a copy of a nonexistent object, no token is created. This applies here because the manifested card, when it died, was not Lightning Bolt, and thus there is no "Lightning Bolt" card exiled with Mimic Vat to copy. Mimic Vat ruling #0 also states that you can't create a token that is a copy of a nonpermanent card, and no token is created in this case.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both creatures exiled by Fiend Hunter and the copy of its ability will return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. The Lithoform Engine copies Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability, and this copy is also linked to Fiend Hunter's leaves-the-battlefield ability. Therefore, when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, both the original ability and its copy will trigger, returning both exiled creatures. This is because, according to the rules for linked abilities, if an ability is linked to a second ability, copies of that first ability are also linked to that second ability. In this case, Fiend Hunter's ability that exiles a creature is linked to its ability that returns the exiled card to the battlefield. When the Lithoform Engine copies the exiling ability, the copy is also linked to the returning ability. As a result, both exiled creatures are returned to the battlefield under their owner's control.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. Teferi's Protection causes your permanents, including Banishing Light, to phase out. Banishing Light's ability exiles a permanent until Banishing Light leaves the battlefield. Since Banishing Light is phased out, it is treated as though it doesn't exist and is not on the battlefield. Therefore, the condition for the exiled creature to return (Banishing Light leaving the battlefield) is not met. Additionally, rulings for Teferi's Protection state that one-shot effects waiting "until [this] leaves the battlefield" do not happen when a permanent phases out.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text: Your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell. Emrakul, the Promised End has "protection from instants" [702.16b]. However, protection abilities only apply while the object with the ability is on the battlefield [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]. Since Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack when your opponent casts Counterspell targeting it, its protection from instants does not prevent it from being targeted. If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the Promised End, Emrakul, the Promised End will be put into its owner's graveyard [608.2n]. The cast trigger of Emrakul, the Promised End would not resolve, and therefore you would not gain control of your opponent during their next turn, nor would they take an extra turn.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text: Yes, Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit, but you cannot cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face for free. When a double-faced card is cast, it is by default cast with its front face up [712.11a, 712.11c]. The cascade ability checks the mana value of the exiled card to determine if it's a legal hit [702.85a]. Valki, God of Lies has a mana value of 2, which is less than the mana value of a typical cascade spell (which would be higher than 2). Therefore, Valki, God of Lies is a legal card to exile with cascade. However, the cascade ability allows you to cast the exiled card without paying its mana cost only if the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value [702.85a]. The Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face has a mana value of 7, which is not less than the mana value of the cascade spell. Therefore, you cannot cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for free. Additionally, even if you could cast it, the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face would be cast with its back face up [712.11a].

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text: You will control your opponent's next turn, and then that player will take an extra turn after that. You will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End, but copying the spell itself will not give you another control-a-turn trigger. The cast trigger of Emrakul, the Promised End states, "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn." This is a triggered ability. When you copy this triggered ability with Lithoform Engine, you create a second instance of that ability on the stack [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. Both of these abilities will resolve, giving you control of your opponent's next turn and then granting them an extra turn afterward. The second part of your question concerns copying the permanent spell Emrakul, the Promised End. When you copy a spell, it is put onto the stack [707.10d]. A copy of a spell is itself a spell [707.10d]. The ability on Emrakul, the Promised End that states "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent..." is a cast trigger, not a triggered ability that occurs when the spell resolves. Therefore, copying the spell itself does not trigger this ability again. The ability on Emrakul, the Promised End that grants an extra turn is part of the cast trigger, not an effect of the permanent spell itself. Therefore, copying the permanent spell does not grant another extra turn.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you will get two tokens. When you activate Mimic Vat's ability to create a token, that ability goes on the stack. Then, you use Lithoform Engine's ability to copy that activated ability. This results in two abilities on the stack, both of which will resolve and create a token. The first ability to resolve will create a token that is a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat. The second ability to resolve will also create a token that is a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat. This is because a copy of an ability copies its characteristics and any decisions made for it, including targets [707.10b, 707.2a]. The ability of Mimic Vat refers to "a card exiled with this artifact," and if that ability is copied, the copy also refers to "a card exiled with this artifact" [707.10b]. If multiple cards were exiled with Mimic Vat, the controller of the copy would choose which card to copy for that copy [607.3]. However, in this scenario, the original ability and its copy both refer to the same exiled card, resulting in two identical tokens being created.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text: If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0 while your opponent controls an untapped Trinisphere and you have a permanent that makes your green spells cost {1} less, the total cost to cast Awaken the Woods will be {2}{G}. You will create zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. To cast Awaken the Woods for its awaken ability, you should choose X=3. If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=3, the mana cost is {3}{G}{G}. Your permanent reduces the cost by {1}, making the cost {2}{G}{G}. Trinisphere then applies, increasing the cost to {3}{G}{G} because the mana component of the cost ({2}{G}{G}) is less than three mana. You will create three 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. The awaken ability itself requires paying the awaken cost, which is {X}{G}{G} [702.113a]. If you choose to pay the awaken cost, you would pay {3}{G}{G} for X=3, and then Trinisphere would apply to that cost. However, the question asks about casting Awaken the Woods for value, implying the use of its awaken ability. The awaken ability is a spell ability that is part of the spell itself [702.113a]. When casting a spell with an {X} in its mana cost, the controller chooses the value of X as part of casting the spell [107.3a]. The mana value of Awaken the Woods is 2, regardless of the value of X [202.3e]. When casting Awaken the Woods with X=0, the mana cost is {0}{G}{G}. Your permanent reduces this to {G}{G}. Trinisphere then applies, increasing the cost to {3} because the mana component of the cost ({G}{G}) is less than three mana. The total cost becomes {3}. You will create zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens [702.113a]. To get the most value from Awaken the Woods, you should choose X=3. The mana cost is {3}{G}{G}. Your permanent reduces this to {2}{G}{G}. Trinisphere then applies, increasing the cost to {3}{G}{G} because the mana component of the cost ({2}{G}{G}) is less than three mana. The total cost is {3}{G}{G}. You will create three 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens [702.113a].

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard to the battlefield with Animate Dead. When Animate Dead enters the battlefield, it will return Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control and attach itself to Grist, the Hunger Tide. Because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card in your graveyard, it can be targeted by Animate Dead. According to the card data for Grist, the Hunger Tide, anywhere but on the battlefield, it is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect. This means it is a creature card and can be targeted by Animate Dead. When Grist, the Hunger Tide enters the battlefield this way, it will no longer be a creature and will be just a planeswalker, as per its card data. If Animate Dead leaves the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide's controller will sacrifice it.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Skullbriar, the Walking Grave does not keep its counters when it moves to the command zone. When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave re-enters the battlefield, Doubling Season will double any counters it would enter with. 

Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another [122.2]. The counters are not "removed"; they simply cease to exist [122.2]. This rule has exceptions, but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's ability states that counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library. However, the command zone is not the battlefield, so the counters would cease to exist when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave moves to the command zone. 

When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave re-enters the battlefield, if an effect would put one or more counters on it, Doubling Season will put twice that many of those counters on it instead [Doubling Season ruling #2]. This is because Doubling Season's effect applies to permanents that enter with counters [Doubling Season ruling #2].

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game. When you activate Sundial of the Infinite's ability during your extra turn, it ends the turn before the end step is reached. Since the end step is skipped, the triggered ability that causes you to lose the game at the beginning of that turn's end step does not trigger. This is because the game skips straight to the cleanup step, and "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities do not trigger if the end step is skipped [724.1e]. The ruling for Final Fortune also states that if you skip the extra turn gained, you do not lose the game [Final Fortune ruling #1].

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: When you cast Clone, you choose what it copies as part of the process of putting it onto the battlefield. This choice is made as Clone enters the battlefield, not when it is cast. Clone has an ability that reads, "You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield." This is an "enters the battlefield" ability, and the choice is made when the permanent is entering the battlefield. Your opponent can respond to the spell Clone after you cast it, but before it enters the battlefield. They cannot respond to the choice of what Clone copies, as that choice is made as it enters the battlefield. If they respond to the Clone spell, their spell or ability will resolve before Clone enters the battlefield and you make your choice. If they respond to Clone entering the battlefield, they can do so before you make your choice. Rule [707.5] states that an object that enters the battlefield "as a copy" of another object becomes a copy as it enters the battlefield. Rule [707.6] states that if an object enters the battlefield as a copy of another permanent, the object's controller will get to make any "as [this] enters the battlefield" choices for it. Clone's ability is an "as enters the battlefield" ability. Rule [Clone ruling #2] clarifies that Clone can only copy a creature that is already on the battlefield when Clone enters. Rule [Clone ruling #0] states that Clone's ability does not target the chosen creature.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text: You will get one land from activating Flooded Strand. Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability copies activated or triggered abilities that are on the stack [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. The ability of Flooded Strand is an activated ability that, when activated, searches your library for a Plains or Island card and puts it onto the battlefield. When Gogo, Master of Mimicry copies this ability, it creates additional instances of that ability on the stack [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. However, the ability of Flooded Strand does not create any lands; it searches for a land and puts it onto the battlefield. Therefore, even with the copies, you only get one land from the original Flooded Strand activation.
